## Summary

I reviewed all 10 source files plus checked for dependency metadata (none present).

**Findings (3 exploitable):**

1. **`authentication-bypass` (CRITICAL)** — `src/oauth/token.js` + `src/oauth/jwks.js`: `verifyExternalToken` fetches the JWT verification key from the attacker-controlled `header.jku` JOSE field. The only guard, `String(url).startsWith('https://keys.example.test')`, is a string prefix check bypassable via `https://keys.example.test@evil.com/x` (userinfo) or `https://keys.example.test.evil.com/x` (subdomain). An attacker hosts their own public key, forges a JWT signed with the matching private key, and the server accepts it — full authentication bypass.

2. **`ssrf` (HIGH)** — Same `fetchKey` code path: the prefix-only check plus `redirect: 'follow'` lets an attacker point the server-side fetch at internal/link-local targets (e.g. `169.254.169.254` metadata) — either directly via userinfo/subdomain tricks or via a 302 redirect.

3. **`open-redirect` (HIGH)** — `src/oauth/register.js`: `validateRedirect` uses `redirectUri.startsWith(client.baseUrl)` with `baseUrl = 'https://portal.example.test'`. Same prefix-bypass classes let an attacker register `https://portal.example.test.evil.com/cb` or `https://portal.example.test@evil.com/cb` as a "valid" redirect URI, capturing the OAuth authorization code. The sibling `exact-redirect.js` shows the correct exact-match approach but is not used.

**Reviewed and clean (decoys / non-exploitable):** `config.js`, `logging.js`, `http/safe-jwks.js` (fixed URL, `redirect: 'manual'` — the safe counterpart), `exact-redirect.js`, `pkce.js`, `state.js` (timing-safe compare). No secrets, SQL, command, path, deserialization, XSS, CORS, SSTI, prototype-pollution, or dependency issues found.
